newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to plug single market holes in time for EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU to plug single market holes in time for EMU.

text.p: The European Commission, seeking to boost growth and jobs, proposed on Wednesday an ambitious three-stage plan to complete the European Union's single market in time for the launch of monetary union.
The plan, which seeks to remove remaining barriers in the world's largest internal market, will be presented to European Union leaders meeting in Amsterdam on June 16-17.

The EU executive said it would seek renewed political commitment from the 15 member states to move "decisively" towards a true single market by January 1, 1999 -- six years after the original deadline.
"An efficient single market means more jobs. The completion of the single market and the introduction of a single currency go hand in hand," Commission President Jacques Santer said.
EU leaders would not only be asked to endorse the plan in Amsterdam but also to approve "the specific work programme necessary to achieve this objective," Santer added.

The EU launched the original single market programme in 1985 to create a huge domestic market to help European firms compete on world markets by removing all barriers to the free movement of goods, services, capital and people.
But, Santer told a press conference, "the European internal market still isn't working like a proper internal market."
EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Montin said: "The single market will always need revisions, updating, taking care of emerging sectors."
The plan is focused on the management of the single market and includes fewer legislative proposals than the 1985 programme.

A key Commission target is for member states to apply and enforce properly existing single market rules, for example those affecting government contracts, which account for 11.5 percent of the EU's gross domestic product.

To step up pressure on offending member states, it wants to publish regularly a "single market scoreboard" showing how well each country is complying with EU rules, including the number of complaints and infringement cases against it.

The Commission outlined a three-phase approach, reflecting the fact that some of the proposed measures, especially those concerning more tax coordination, may be difficult for EU member states to agree by 1999.
It implicitly acknowledged the difficulties involved, saying that it was essential the EU take all steps necessary to find the "maximum possible agreement" by 1999.

The first phase includes single market actions which do not require new legislation and can be put in place quickly, for example the implementation and enforcement of existing single market rules and liberalisation of telecommunications.
The second phase covers measures that have already been proposed but which still have not been adopted, for example the European Company Statute on worker rights.

The last phase includes measures "where work is less advanced or where progress is likely to prove more difficult," such as a package to increase tax coordination -- an area where member states have failed to agree in the past.
The Commission also said it would put forward a series of single market proposals this year, for example legislation to phase out restrictions on investments by pension funds.
